Raise your average ticket immediately and defer purchasing the second van for the next 90 days. 

Your current van operates 26 days a month, completing 156 grooms. At $95 per groom, monthly revenue is $14,820. Variable costs total $5,070 for labor and $1,872 for supplies and fuel. Subtracting your $3,800 fixed costs leaves a monthly net profit of $4,078. With high demand and a three-and-a-half-week backlog, you have strong pricing power.

In the next 90 days, implement a two-step change. First, raise your base price by 15 percent, moving the average ticket to roughly $110. For regulars who rebook every six to eight weeks, offer a loyalty rate of $100 to protect retention. This captures higher revenue from new or infrequent clients while honoring your core base. Assuming a slight dip in volume to 140 grooms a month, revenue rises to about $15,100, significantly expanding profit margins without adding capital expenditure.

Second, wait on the second van. Financing adds $1,650 plus higher insurance, maintenance, and variable costs, risking margin dilution if early utilization lags. A two-month hiring lag also delays returns. 

Instead, use the next 90 days to test price elasticity and accumulate cash. If the higher pricing sustains full utilization and your waitlist stabilizes, commit to the second van at the end of the quarter. 

Assumptions include steady local demand and stable fuel costs. Decision criteria to buy the van sooner include maintaining at least 95 percent capacity at the new $110 price point and securing reliable groomers before capital commitment.
